How five siblings create Brand New Land's distinctive 'heirloom' landed homes
article:
The siblings who run boutique landed property developer Brand New Land Group grew up with a retelling of an old Chinese folk tale about five brothers, each born with a different extraordinary ability, who take turns helping one of their own using their individual gifts.

The story is one the Teh siblings still return to when they talk about how five of the nine children in their family found themselves in the real estate business together.

"One by one, the universe pulled everybody else in," Alvina Teh, the company's managing director and the fourth-eldest of the nine siblings, tells EdgeProp Singapore .

She started Brand New Land on her own before siblings Tatiana, Al-Emporio, Truman-Sol and Al-Olympia came on board one at a time over the next few years.

Alvina leads strategy and development, Tatiana is design and hospitality director, while Al-Emporio is branding and marketing director. Truman-Sol is project management director, and Al-Olympia is business operations director.

Brand New Land closed its first sale in 2019, and has since developed 25 landed homes, with more than a dozen other projects in progress.

Right people at the right time

The venture began with three homes and a decision to simply give property development a shot.

"We actually didn't have a game plan when we started out," Alvina says. "The opportunity was there, so we thought, 'Let's just do it.'"

Family and friends were encouraging of the first three homes, and their support helped the team move on to its next round of developments.

To Alvina, the five of them ending up in business together was serendipitous — with the right people, timing, mindset and opportunities coming together.

Each sibling stepped in as the business grew and a need arose that matched their strengths.

"As and when a function came up, we just so happened to have someone who could very appropriately fill those shoes," says Al-Emporio.

For instance, the first to join Alvina was Tatiana, who came in as chief creative officer — the creative force behind the homes to oversee design, hospitality and sales.

With more developments in the works, marketing became a greater priority, which was when Al-Emporio came on board as chief marketing officer.

Truman-Sol joined then as chief operating officer when the team needed someone hands-on to lead on construction and project management.

This was followed by Al-Olympia, who took charge of relationships with homebuyers and partners, with the title of chief heart officer.

"We’re quite blessed because we all bring on different strengths," says Al-Emporio.

Tatiana adds: "If you put us in any kind of situation, we will be able to sail through together."

How their upbringing carries into their homes

The siblings' experience of growing up in a large family has influenced the design and layout of Brand New Land's homes.

The houses are intended to naturally draw residents out of their own zones and towards shared spaces where they can spend time together.

Food preparation areas, for example, are closely connected to dining spaces to encourage family members to cook and eat together. The aim is also to make them "as beautiful a space as we possibly can", so people enjoy spending time there, Alvina says.

"It's not just sharing meals but also preparing meals together. A simple act like cooking with family members can really help build a shared life," she adds.

At the same time, their childhood taught the siblings the importance of having space to themselves, even in a household where so many moments are shared.

This is reflected in the meditative corners and private spaces they now incorporate into Brand New Land’s projects — features that were also part of their childhood home life.

"After everybody comes together for a meal, you retreat back into your own sanctuary, your room," Tatiana says. "So, even our designs revolve around how we grew up. And we’re always learning."

Their approach to space has changed over the years as Brand New Land developed more homes.

Alvina recalls they initially followed the conventional playbook that "bigger is better". That has evolved into thinking more about how each space can support the kind of life they envisage for the homes.

Brand New Land's newer projects also take inspiration from Blue Zones — regions around the world known for their populations' longer, healthier lives — and nature.

“We try to do that in a more scientific way,” Alvina says. She adds that they look at how a home can encourage movement, connection with nature and other people, while “celebrating little rituals” such as sharing meals, spending time together and slowing down.

"While we still deliver homes with as generous sizes as possible, we do it only if that extra space really adds meaningful value and enables better lives," Alvina explains.

Longevity and wellness through design

These Blue Zone influences also align with the emerging concept of longevity architecture, which considers how buildings and interiors can actively support health and wellbeing over the long term.

Longevity architecture can encompass factors such as natural light and ventilation, temperature, acoustics, materials and biophilic design.

"When it comes to longevity and wellness, many people think about leaving their homes to go for saunas, cold plunges, and so on," Tatiana says.

Brand New Land instead aims to weave in elements of longevity architecture into the house, including in the lighting, temperature and materials.

"Your home becomes a machine for living, for longevity," Tatiana continues.

At the Solstice project along Tan Sim Boh Road in District 11, this includes the use of natural timber and travertine-inspired tiles, certain colours in rooms that help occupants sleep better, wood-grain screens to soften the facade, and a dark stone base to ground the space.

A collection of four freehold terraced houses tucked within the Chancery landed residential enclave, the three-storey development also features a reflective pool, Zen stone garden and flexible home gym. The spaces are designed to create a sense of calm and tranquility throughout each home.

Solstice was launched in June with asking prices of $9.38 million to $23.28 million. That works out to about $4,406 psf to $4,764 psf based on land area.

Meanwhile, the firm's latest project Pangolins — a pair of freehold semi-detached houses on Jalan Labu Manis in District 19 — likewise emphasises rest and personal space.

Inspired by the pangolin's armour, both five-storey semi-detached houses have a sturdy protective exterior, juxtaposed with a soft interior. Residents can turn inwards to "renew, recharge and re-energise" as a retreat from the world, Tatiana says.

Meditation corners, contemplation decks, reflection terraces, outdoor jacuzzis and sculptural gardens are among its defining features.

Situated at Bartley Rise Estate, Pangolins debuted for sale at end-July, with the smaller house going for $8.5 million or about $3,673 psf based on land area. The adjacent property is priced at $8.8 million or $3,241 psf.

Identity and sense of place

When asked which of their earlier developments stands out to them, Panther — a freehold five-storey semi-detached home — comes readily to mind.

The one-of-a-kind project, which sits on Old Upper Thomson Road in District 20, gave the team greater conviction in the role that identity and storytelling could play in their work.

Built on a sunken plot nestled within lush greenery at the edge of a reservoir, the Panther house evokes the elusive presence of its namesake animal.

The site's lower elevation and designer timber-effect screens contribute to a sense of privacy and seclusion. Two naturally ventilated basement levels and "almost cave-like spaces" add to its hidden, mysterious character, says Alvina.

Moreover, private balconies open the home to its natural surroundings, allowing occupants to soak in the sounds of nature and fresh air from the nearby nature reserve.

"We were quite new back then and tried something more daring," Alvina shares.

The spacious semi-detached house, with about 8,000 sq ft of built-up area, was sold promptly in late 2022 even before its official launch.

The eventual buyer appeared to connect immediately with the house. "We get the sense that when he saw it, he felt, 'This home is me'," Alvina says.

The experience with Panther affirmed the team’s belief in creating homes with a distinct identity and sense of belonging. "Features compete, but identity doesn't," Alvina adds.

Al-Emporio similarly calls Panther a hallmark project, as it helped solidify the team’s belief that evocative storytelling can connect a home with the right buyer, even if it may not resonate with everyone.

In developing such a unique identity for each project, they also consider the character and surroundings of each site, so homes in different parts of Singapore can take on markedly different designs and concepts.

"The ideas are not just plucked out of thin air," Al-Emporio says. "We look at what the location has to offer, to create a sense of place."

She adds that each house is designed to fit its surroundings while still being striking, without appearing "too loud" or jarring to the environment.

Choosing the right sites for 'heirloom' homes

This attention to the surroundings and sense of place guides how they select sites to acquire.

On top of the general location and the neighbourhood's character, the team also considers the immediate environment such as noise and activity levels around a site, and what the plot will allow them to create.

For example, the land on which Panther was built had been passed over by many other developers and buyers mainly because it sits below street level.

But the team saw potential in the double-basement concept and the chance to make the most of the treetop views right by the reservoir.

Brand New Land is also willing to pay more for established locations with character and lasting appeal, while passing over sites that might be priced favourably but fall short of their criteria.

"We'd rather say no to 10 sites than say yes to the wrong one," Alvina says.

"Sometimes, a home has a really attractive price, but we won’t be able to deliver a lifestyle centred around Blue Zone behaviours for wellness and longevity if the site is too noisy or busy. Or it could be surrounded by too many negative attributes," she adds.

The developer also focuses exclusively on freehold and 999-year leasehold land, taking a long-term view of the homes it builds and their enduring value.

Alvina refers to Brand New Land's homes as "heirloom" properties that can potentially be held and passed down through generations.

Relationships behind each home

The Tehs' family dynamic has carried into the working relationships behind Brand New Land’s developments, from builders to buyers.

In a household with nine siblings, there were plenty of personalities to contend with, especially when the children had "no filters", as Alvina puts it.

Having to learn to tolerate, respect and understand one another was therefore akin to an education in itself — one that prepared the siblings not only for working together, but also for managing the myriad relationships involved in each project.

Tatiana uses the term "relationship hospitality" to describe how Brand New Land works closely with different parties.

This thinking applies throughout the development process. Alvina points out that every interaction with consultants, contractors, suppliers and partners contributes to the quality of the final product.

The team is likewise hands-on with buyers, including engaging directly with them from the first touchpoint, when someone reaches out to enquire about a home.

"Everybody wants to feel seen and heard," Tatiana notes. "So for us, it’s very important to be there with them to let them know what’s happening and what comes next."

She believes this level of involvement makes a meaningful difference and adds value to the overall homebuying experience.

Some homeowners have even gone on to become investors in Brand New Land's projects and advocates for the company, to the team’s pleasant surprise.

Watching a community form around the brand and "take on a life of its own" has brought a new and "very heartening level" of support, Alvina says.

"It tells us to just keep going, keep delivering, and be true to ourselves. Our responsibility then becomes to remain authentic, because other people are believing in us too," she adds.

Next slate of unique landed homes

Their upcoming launches continue in that vein, with each development taking on an identity informed by its location, surroundings and the team's focus on longevity and wellbeing.

Azurean, a semi-detached house in Bukit Timah, will have a yacht-inspired aesthetic, with whites, blues and neutral tones, floor-to-ceiling windows and abundant sunlight.

The 999-year leasehold property is located along Ming Teck Park, off Sixth Avenue.

"A lot of residents in the neighbourhood love their boats," says Tatiana. The yacht theme was the first thing that came to her mind when she visited Azurean's site.

"White, blue, travertine, beige; all these elements coming together. I thought, 'This is going to be beautiful over here'," Tatiana adds.

Another Bukit Timah project, a bungalow named Clos Arvo along Coronation Road West, features a European flair as it takes its cues from French vineyards.

Meanwhile, 29, a corner terrace at 29 Everitt Road in the East Coast area, will have a Chinoiserie-influenced modern heritage aesthetic.

Equinox, a collection of four semi-detached homes situated along Tan Sim Boh Road near Solstice, will combine influences from luxury resorts, Japanese spatial design, tropical modernism and monastic architecture.

The concept for Equinox seeks to create a slower, calmer experience through its use of shadow, texture, sound, air, water and silence.

"Each of the houses is very, very different," Tatiana says.

These four projects — Azurean, Clos Arvo, 29 and Equinox — are expected to be launched in 2026 and 2027, ahead of completion in the second half of 2028.

One home at a time

With a solid pipeline ahead, the Tehs say the priority is to stay focused on what is in front of them.

Alvina points to the company’s purpose of "enriching lives, one home at a time", which serves as a reminder to give their best to each home and the people involved.

That focus also gives the siblings a common point to return to when disagreements and different perspectives inevitably arise.

"Whenever we disagree or have different ways of seeing things, we always recentre ourselves by returning to our shared vision for the company," says Al-Emporio.

"It boils down to respecting one another and wanting to push for the same thing at the end of the day," she adds. "All disagreements then fall away."

The ability to work through differences has been honed over a lifetime while growing up together.

Alvina jokes that learning how to get along and put up with one another was "a matter of survival, for our sanity".

She describes the five siblings as essentially "stuck with each other" for life.

In a business where projects can take years to come to fruition, they have the advantage of knowing they can count on one another to see things through together.

title: Freehold Geylang redevelopment site for sale at $33 mil
article:
A freehold plot at 30 and 32 Lorong 22 Geylang has been launched for sale at a guide price of $33 million, or $928 psf per plot ratio.

The 12,693 sq ft site is zoned for commercial/institution use with an allowable plot ratio of 2.8. It is currently occupied by two three-storey apartment blocks comprising 12 units.

According to SRI Capital Market, which is handling the sale, the site can be redeveloped into a commercial building, entertainment hub or recreation club. Other potential uses include a commercial school or community institution, subject to approval from the relevant authorities.

“The zoning provides prospective buyers with greater flexibility in considering the property’s future redevelopment potential,” says Low Choon Sin, managing partner of SRI Capital Market.

Located off Guillemard Road, the site is close to commercial, recreational and community amenities, including KFF Badminton Arena and Kallang Sports Hub, as well as several religious institutions.

The site could also benefit from rejuvenation plans in the wider Kallang precinct under the Kallang Alive Masterplan, which aims to strengthen the area as a lifestyle and recreational destination.

“The property is well positioned to appeal to investors, owner-occupiers and developers seeking a freehold redevelopment site with multiple potential end-use possibilities, while benefiting from the established amenities and activity in the Geylang precinct,” says Bruce Lye, managing partner of SRI.

The public tender for 30 and 32 Lorong 22 Geylang will close on Sept 22 at 3pm.

title: Living in a 'haunted' home? Four ways feng shui could help
article:
A home where someone has died suddenly or unnaturally can be unsettling, even for people who do not usually believe in the supernatural.

It can be especially unnerving for homebuyers who discover only after completing their purchase that their new home has such a history — or who begin to suspect something is amiss only after moving in.

Over the years, I have been called to such homes across Singapore, from HDB flats, condos and apartments to landed houses.

Some homes have a known history of death or tragedy. Others approach me only after experiencing things they struggle to explain — disturbed sleep, a feeling of being watched, sightings of figures, or lights and appliances behaving strangely despite repeated checks.

In Chinese, a property associated with a violent, sudden or unnatural death is commonly described as a xiong zhai , or literally an inauspicious or ominous dwelling.

From a feng shui perspective, such an event may leave behind strong yin or residual energy associated with distress, regret or resentment, affecting how comfortable and settled the subsequent occupants feel in the home.

But there is no need to be afraid of a xiong zhai . A property’s negative history does not mean it has to forever remain an inauspicious place to live.

There are certainly religious approaches to dealing with such homes, including chanting, prayers, talismans and other rites. But these vary according to one’s faith and religious practices, and are separate from the feng shui methods I want to focus on here.

From a feng shui perspective, there are typically four physical approaches:

1. Interrupting a problematic passage between doors and windows; 2. Replacing materials at the location associated with a death; 3. Using sustained bright light to introduce yang energy; 4. And, in more serious cases, changing the orientation of the home's entrance.

The appropriate method depends on the property, its history and where the problem is concentrated.

Start with the conditions in the home

In feng shui, yin and yang are complementary forces. Yin is associated with qualities such as darkness, stillness and coolness, while yang is associated with brightness, warmth and activity.

Neither is inherently undesirable. A bedroom, for example, naturally requires more yin qualities than a busy living area. However, problems can sometimes arise when a home or a particular part of it becomes excessively dark, still or stagnant.

This is why I pay attention to more than the history of a property, to look at its doors and windows, natural light and airflow, as well as the location where an incident is believed to have taken place.

A dark staircase that receives almost no daylight may require a different solution from a specific spot where an unnatural death occurred.

Unexplained occurrences also do not automatically mean that a home is "haunted" or that whatever is present must be malicious.

Breaking a 'yin passage'

One condition to look out for is called a chuan tang yin lu , or a "yin passage" through the home.

This can occur where a door and window sit in a direct line, creating an uninterrupted passage through the property. In a home already associated with an unnatural death or other disturbance, I would want to break this alignment.

One method is to install a heavy, dark red curtain at the window at the other end of the passage. The curtain interrupts the direct connection, while its colour introduces a strong yang element.

I would also open the windows throughout the home between about 11am and 1pm and allow fresh air to circulate. Traditionally, midday is regarded as the period when yang energy is at its strongest.

Moving air helps disperse stagnant yin energy accumulated in a poorly ventilated space that is kept closed or dark for long periods.

The idea is to change those physical conditions by letting in air, light and movement.

'Changing the bones' of an affected space

Where a suicide, accidental death or other unnatural death has occurred at an identifiable location within the home, it might call for a more extensive intervention.

This is known as huan gu , or literally "changing the bones".

It involves removing the floor and wall finishes within a roughly 1.5m radius of the location associated with the incident.

Instead of covering the area or replacing it with exactly the same finishes, I prefer to change the material where possible. Timber might be replaced with tile or masonry, for example, or vice versa.

This process can also be described as bo pi , or "peeling away the skin". Removing and replacing the old materials can change the physical environment at that spot.

Afterwards, it would be ideal to burn mugwort, together with coarse salt, at the affected area.

Salt can counter yin energy, while mugwort is associated with introducing yang energy and purification.

If an intense event has become associated with a particular spot, we should not simply hide it under a new coat of paint. The space itself will need to change.

Bringing yang into the home through light

Another method for such residences is known as yi guang dai huo — using light to introduce the yang qualities traditionally associated with fire.

In a particularly dark or affected area, the homeowner may install an extremely bright LED light and keep it illuminated continuously, or for prescribed hours each day, for 49 consecutive days.

The number 49, or seven cycles of seven days, has longstanding cultural and spiritual associations with death and transition in Chinese traditions. In feng shui, it can represent a complete period of change for a space.

Strong white light can disrupt an excessively yin environment and introduce sustained yang energy.

The method may sound surprisingly mundane as compared to incense, talismans or religious objects, but in certain homes, what I bring is simply an LED light.

A figure on the staircase in a Serangoon Gardens home

In March this year, I received a call from the owner of a landed house in Serangoon Gardens.

A family of four had lived there for three years, but the owner said the atmosphere had changed noticeably over the past two months.

Their child had begun waking and crying in the middle of the night, saying someone was standing at the doorway. Both husband and wife also found themselves waking at 3am sharp every night, with the nagging feeling that somebody was standing beside the bed, watching them.

What caught my attention most was that their daughter reported seeing a woman wearing a floral dress, repeatedly walking back and forth on the staircase.

When I visited, I noticed how little natural light entered parts of the house. The interior felt dark and the staircase was especially poorly lit.

I asked the owners whether anyone had previously fallen on the stairs. They were surprised by the question, before saying that the previous owner’s elderly mother had fallen there. She died about six months later.

My interpretation was that the woman whom the child had described was not there to harm them. I believed she was trapped at the staircase, with her consciousness or residual presence repeatedly returning to the moment of the fall.

The solution I recommended was simple: a 10,000-lumen bright LED light in the stairwell.

The family switched it on from 4pm until the next morning for 49 consecutive days; any interrupting meant restarting the count.

The objective was to counter the prolonged darkness and excess yin energy accumulated in the space by flooding it with sustained light.

The owner later told me that the child stopped waking and crying at night shortly after the light treatment began, while his wife was able to sleep through the night again.

In feng shui, bringing light into an area where yin energy has become too strong can help introduce yang energy and restore balance.

When an old habit lingers, at a Holland-Bukit Timah house

Another case, this time at a large landed property in the Holland-Bukit Timah area, presented very differently.

The homeowners were a young couple working in finance who said they did not believe in the supernatural. Yet they had encountered a problem they could not explain.

Every night at 8pm, the light in their living room would apparently switch itself on.

As they rarely used the living room at night, the wife made a point of checking that its light was turned off before going to bed. When she came out of the bedroom later, however, she would find it switched on again.

This happened repeatedly, even after the couple replaced the switches and the electrical distribution board or DB box. Electricians who were called in several times found the bungalow’s electrical system functioning normally, according to the couple.

When I visited, I focused on the home’s layout and physical conditions.

A large tree outside the west-facing balcony substantially blocked the light, leaving the living room with little natural illumination once the sun set.

I would describe the condition as chen — a sense of heaviness or stagnation. Light was being obstructed, and the circulation of qi had also become sluggish.

The couple told me the previous owner was an elderly man. After he died, the property stood vacant for about two years before they purchased it.

I asked whether the elderly man had habitually switched on the living-room light every evening. The couple later found out that he had.

As with the Serangoon Gardens case, I did not see anything malicious. I regarded what was happening as the residue of the former owner’s old routine.

I suggested a similar light-based approach: a 5,000K LED, which is a crisp neutral white light similar to natural midday sunlight, kept illuminated for 49 days.

The light served two purposes. It brought continuous brightness into a space where natural light had been obstructed, while also helping the previous occupant recognise that the property had already changed hands and it was time to leave.

After the treatment ended, the living room light stopped switching itself on.

Changing the home's orientation

Last but not least, the most extensive — and, in my view, often the most potent — of the four methods is gai men huan xiang .

This refers to altering the entrance and changing the facing direction of the home.

Traditional feng shui goes further than the four main directions of north, south, east and west. One important system uses the 24 Mountains, dividing the compass into 24 directional sectors of 15 degrees each.

A property's zuo xiang — its sitting and facing direction — helps determine how it receives and interacts with qi.

The 24 Mountains system names these more precise compass directions: zi and wu , for example, correspond broadly to north and south, while chou and wei correspond to north-northeast and south-southwest.

A home described as zuo zi xiang wu therefore sits to the north and faces south. By adjusting the angle of its entrance, the house could potentially be changed to another orientation, zuo chou xiang wei , sitting north-northeast and facing south-southwest.

These are distinct orientations associated with different patterns of qi. Changing from one to the other therefore changes the energy the home receives.

This intervention is much more drastic than opening windows, replacing finishes or installing a light.

It will not be physically or legally possible in every property, depending on the housing type, layout and renovation restrictions. Homeowners should first check what alterations are permitted before changing the position or angle of the front door.

A home's past need not determine its future

A property where someone has died unnaturally will understandably make some buyers and residents uncomfortable. Others may become worried only after encountering experiences they cannot explain.

But I do not believe such homes have to remain inauspicious or unsettling.

The key is to understand the property's conditions and what could be contributing to the problem.

Nor should every unexplained presence be assumed to be hostile or "unclean". At times, what lingers might be traces of what happened — or who lived there — before.

The aim is then not to forcibly chase it away, but to let it know there is no longer a need to stay and that it is all right to move on.

A home's history cannot be changed, but its feng shui can.

With the appropriate intervention, a xiong zhai with an unfortunate past can still become a place where its next occupants feel settled and at ease.

title: Meta Platforms vs OCBC: Which Stock Creates More Value for Shareholders?
article:
You don’t have to stick to same-sector comparisons to find great investment opportunities.
Take
Meta Platforms, Inc
(NASDAQ: META) and
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited
(SGX: O39), or OCBC, for example.
Meta turns digital attention and ad space into profit, whereas OCBC earns income through traditional banking.
Though their business engines are total opposites, their destination is the same: creating strong cash flows or profits to reinvest in the business or pay out to shareholders through dividends and
buybacks
.
This article compares how each company creates value for shareholders.
Different Business Models, Different Paths to Shareholder Returns
Meta Platforms
Meta
operates one of the world’s largest social media ecosystems, including Facebook, Instagram, Messenger and WhatsApp.
Its business is primarily powered by digital advertising, which contributed US$59.4 billion, or nearly 98% of 2Q2026 revenue (total revenue: US$60.8 billion).
The tech giant benefits from strong software economics, as the incremental cost of serving additional users is relatively low.
Its massive scale and strong operating margins help the company convert a large portion of its earnings into cash.
In the first half of 2026 (1H2026), operating cash flow grew 29.2% year on year (YoY), from US$49.6 billion to US$64.1 billion.
However, Meta’s push into artificial intelligence (AI) is making the business increasingly capital-intensive.
The company spent US$49.1 billion on property and equipment in 1H2026 to expand its infrastructure, a 66.4% YoY increase from US$29.5 billion.
As a result, Meta generated US$13.2 billion in free cash flow, a 30.3% decline from a year earlier.
On a trailing 12-month basis, its free cash flow fell 20.4% YoY to US$37.9 billion.
Management expects 2026’s capital expenditure to be between US$130 billion and US$145 billion.
Right now, the social media giant is prioritising the future by pouring cash into AI infrastructure and research.
But even with these big-ticket investments, Meta’s financial health remains rock-solid, backed by US$90.3 billion in cash and marketable securities as of end-June 2026.
Having that kind of cash pile gives Meta ultimate flexibility – meaning it has more than enough firepower to make strategic investments while returning capital via buybacks and dividends.
OCBC
OCBC
generates value differently.
It does so through consumer and corporate banking, wealth management, and insurance.
And in the banking business, investors should focus on profitability, the balance sheet, and regulatory strength.
For 1H2026, net interest income fell 3% YoY to S$4.5 billion as lower interest rates weighed on margins.
However, non-interest income jumped 36% YoY to a record S$3.5 billion, supported by higher fee, trading and insurance income.
This led to an 11% increase in total income to S$8.0 billion.
With operating expenses rising at a slower pace, OCBC’s net profit for 1H2026 was up 13% YoY to S$4.2 billion.
OCBC’s balance sheet looks strong with a non-performing loan ratio of just 0.9%, a 78.4% loan-to-deposit ratio, and a leverage ratio of 6.5%.
Because of its solid earnings and balance sheet, OCBC can easily fund new loans while returning extra capital to shareholders.
But it also plays it safe.
OCBC retains enough cash reserves to meet strict regulatory rules and fuel ongoing investments in digital technology, regional growth, and client relationships.
OCBC’s fully phased-in Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio stood at a strong 14% as of June 2026.
OCBC declared an interim dividend of S$0.47 per share, up 15% YoY, and continues to work towards completing its S$2.5 billion capital return programme by the end of 2026.
Capital Allocation: Two Different Philosophies
Meta and OCBC take very different approaches to capital allocation.
Meta puts growth, innovation, and AI first – management’s focus is on reinvesting in the business.
OCBC takes the classic banking route – steady dividends, prudent risk management, and stable growth.
But at the end of the day, they give investors what they want.
Technology investors demand growth and reinvention, while bank investors look for safety and dependable yield.
Which Type of Investor Might Prefer Each?
Despite operating in totally different industries, both Meta and OCBC provide a masterclass in running a profitable and financially disciplined business that knows how to reinvest for the future.
Instead of using a one-size-fits-all tape measure, look at what each brings to your portfolio.
If you’re looking for capital growth, global tech exposure, and AI upside, Meta fits the bill.
But if you prefer steady earnings, growing dividend income, and a solid foothold in Singapore and Asian banking, OCBC is a natural choice.
And remember, investing isn’t an either/or decision – owning both gives you a balanced mix of growth and income while keeping your portfolio diversified.
Common Mistakes Investors Make
The most common mistake is comparing companies across industries without understanding each company’s underlying business model.
Technology and banking investments can play very
different but complementary roles
within a diversified portfolio.
Get Smart: Different Businesses, Same Goal
Meta and OCBC are very different when it comes to generating shareholder value.
One uses its free cash flow for innovation and buybacks, while the other channels its capital towards loan growth and dividends.
But both reward shareholders.
Together, Meta and OCBC demonstrate how vastly different business models can both effectively build long-term value for a diversified portfolio.

title: Tackling NHS inefficiency could save Britain £32 bil
article:
(Aug 19): The UK Treasury would be as much as £32 billion better off each year if Britain’s government-run health service had kept pace with its pre-pandemic productivity gains, according to analysis of official figures.

The data shows a 26% surge in resources used by the National Health Service from 2019 to 2025 as successive governments tried to turn around ailing frontline services. However, NHS output was up just 19% over the same period.

It leaves productivity lagging well behind pre-Covid-19 levels despite some improvement in recent quarters. If productivity had continued to grow at the pace seen during the 2010s, the government could be spending £31.5 billion less each year on health while achieving the same level of service that it currently provides. Alternatively, the UK could be spending that money to improve the NHS or other public services.

When looking at a wider timescale, the Treasury would be saving over £26 billion a year if NHS productivity had continued at levels seen between 1997 and 2019.

The NHS has long been a hot political issue in Britain. Providing health treatment free at the point of use, it is extremely popular with the public despite discontent around the level of service. The Labour government has been trying to slash backlogs that built up during the pandemic under the previous Conservative administration. However, waiting lists still number more than seven million patients, well above pre-Covid-19 levels.

See also: Caring for Singapore’s frontline staff amid an ageing society

Left-wing Members of Parliament would like to increase health funding even further, yet new Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey has little wriggle room ahead of his first budget in the autumn.

Healey needs to find more money for Britain’s military and some of UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s other ambitions for a more active state.

“We could spend the same amount but spend it more efficiently and effectively,” said Tera Allas, co-chair of the Health Foundation’s NHS Productivity Commission, who analysed the numbers. “I can’t help but look around and see that there’s a ton of ways in which that could be done. Those tons of ways don’t easily match up with the reality of political economy.”

She said under-investment in the NHS’s capital resources is the main reason behind the productivity slowdown as workers lose valuable time dealing with inadequate equipment, waiting for access to machinery or dealing with deteriorating facilities. Allas highlighted a lack of managers who can allocate resources, improve processes, reduce waste and train workers.

The NHS could also cut regulations and prioritise a modern patient-records system to turn things around more quickly. But fundamental changes take time, Allas said, like sustained investment in infrastructure, tech and staff training. “You need to start investing in them now.”

NHS productivity tanked in 2020, after improving for decades, and has still not returned to its pre-Covid-19 path. Capital per worker in the NHS fell 36% between 2010 and 2019 while a £14 billion maintenance backlog makes operations less efficient. During that decade, the UK would have needed to invest £32.9 billion more to keep up with comparable European peers such as France, Austria, Denmark or Greece.

“Not investing in your capital budget in the 2010s doesn’t really look bad in the short term,” said Stuart Hoddinott, associate director at the Institute for Government. “But over the long term, that really builds up into a very bad backlog of problems in your estate and in your capital stock, which makes your staff less productive. That’s the state we’re in now.”

Hoddinott said there may also be a productivity impact from losing experienced staff around the pandemic as well as the prioritisation of frontline hospital resources over other parts of the system, such as social care, mental health services and community care.

title: Kuaishou earnings drop by a third, hit by AI and creator costs
article:
(Aug 19): Kuaishou Technology earnings fell the most in five years, hit by higher revenue sharing payouts to creators while artificial intelligence (AI) outlays drove spending up by more than a third.

Net income slipped 36% to 3.15 billion yuan (US$467 million or $600 million) for the second quarter, the biggest drop since 2021 and marking only the fourth contraction since then.

The cost of both revenue sharing and research and development — which is primarily related to AI spending — rose 35% over the quarter.

Income from its livestreaming business also fell, offsetting most of the growth in its bigger online marketing services business, according to a Wednesday filing. Overall revenue was stable at 35.5 billion yuan, in line with analyst expectations.

Sales growth for Kuaishou’s flagship Kling AI text-to-video also slowed, clocking 200% growth in the second quarter, down from 300% a quarter ago.

See also: SK Hynix moves to calm market with US$29 bil share buy-back

“We are cautious about the short-term business outlook as the operating environment has become increasingly complex and challenging,” the company said. The firm will continue to scale Kling AI’s model capabilities and unlock additional commercialisation opportunities.

Alibaba Group Holding Ltd and Tencent Holdings Ltd are among the clutch of investors that joined a US$2.8 billion ($3.57 billion) financing round for Kling AI. Kling is now part of a wave of Chinese AI video services seeking to pull in revenue from global customers, moving to fill a void after OpenAI shuttered Sora.

title: China’s biggest beauty firm to expand in US with Ulta deal
article:
(Aug19): Proya Cosmetics Co is set to expand in the US market through a partnership with Ulta Beauty Inc as China’s biggest beauty company looks abroad for growth to help it weather fierce competition at home.

Proya is set to launch its flagship Ruby and Original Repair skincare lines in 400 brick-and-mortar Ulta stores as well as on its online platform, the Chinese company said in a statement on its WeChat account. The collaboration represents a significant breakthrough for Proya in its global expansion, it said.

The move marks a rare instance of a Chinese skincare brand achieving mainstream retail distribution in a Western market. While a wave of C-beauty brands, including Florasis and Flower Knows, have gained traction through cross-border e-commerce and growing interest in Asian beauty trends, skincare remains dominated by the likes of L’Oréal SA and Estée Lauder Cos.

The tie-up also gives Proya an important avenue for growth as the domestic market plateaus due to cautious consumer spending and intense price wars. The company’s annual revenue declined about 1.7% in 2025 following years of double-digit growth.

Prior to the Ulta partnership, Hangzhou-based Proya had struck an agreement in April to roll out its star products at Guardian, Malaysia’s leading beauty and personal care retail chain. The deal will see products gradually available across the network of more than 200 physical stores in the Southeast Asian country.

title: US sanctions ICC president and vows to ‘dismantle’ court
article:
(Aug19): The Trump administration announced sanctions on the president and senior trial lawyer of the International Criminal Court, further escalating pressure against an institution that it says has unfairly targeted the US and Israel.

The court is “a corrupt and fatally politicised supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate”, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement. He threatened more measures to “systematically dismantle the ICC until it is incapable of threatening American sovereignty”.

Rubio’s statement and the sanctions targeting ICC president Tomoko Akane, who is from Japan, and Senegal’s Abdoulaye Seye, its senior trial lawyer, amount to the clearest indication yet that the US wants to cripple the institution rather than simply sideline it.

The ICC said in a statement the sanctions were “a flagrant attack against the independence of an impartial judicial institution”. With the latest action, it said that a total of nine of the eighteen ICC judges had been sanctioned by the US, in addition to other staff.

“The Court remains undeterred and stands firmly behind its personnel and behind victims of unimaginable atrocities,” it said, adding that it would “continue to fully discharge its mandate with independence and impartiality”.

Japan issued a statement calling the sanctions against Akane “very unfortunate". While a close US ally, Tokyo is the largest financial backer of the court. “Japan has consistently supported the ICC,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs Press Secretary Toshihiro Kitamura said in the statement, adding the country remained committed to strengthening the rule of law in the international community.

See also: Disney sues FCC over ‘retaliatory campaign’ tied to licences

Trump and his allies have long accused the ICC of interfering in US affairs. During his first term, he slapped sanctions on an ICC prosecutor and one of her aides for investigating accusations of American war crimes in Afghanistan.

The court issued an arrest warrant for Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in 2024 over allegations of war crimes in Gaza. The Israeli government has denied the accusations, and the Biden administration rejected the court’s authority.

Neither the US nor Israel is a party to the court, which was established in 2002 in the Hague, Netherlands, to prosecute war crimes, genocide and other atrocities. It has issued 60 arrest warrants, including for Russian President Vladimir Putin, and has detained 21 people.

See also: Trump appeals ruling against his IRS audit immunity deal

Seye, who was recently nominated to be an ICC judge, has worked on the prosecutorial team of the court’s Israel-Palestine proceedings.

Netherlands Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen condemned the latest action, saying in a social media post that “international courts and tribunals must be able to freely carry out their mandates”.

Last week, four leading US human rights organisations filed a lawsuit over the Trump administration’s campaign against the ICC, arguing the sanctions limit “access to justice for victims of serious international crimes around the globe".

title: Shell trader Mansfield resigns after 26 years at oil major — Bloomberg
article:
(Aug 19): Shell Plc veteran Geoffrey Mansfield has resigned from his role as global desk lead for low-carbon fuels trading, according to a person familiar with the matter.

He joined the oil major’s London trading floor in 2006 and went on to build and manage refined products desks for distillates, gasoline and jet fuel, according to his LinkedIn profile. Shell declined to comment.

Mansfield assumed control of the low-carbon fuels desk almost five years ago, just as the industry entered a period of rapid growth driven by ambitious government mandates for alternatives to conventional fossil fuels. Traders in the sector buy and sell the fuels as well as regulatory credits associated with them.

Shell has scaled back parts of its low-carbon business in recent years, as the broader oil industry pivots away from energy transition assets and back towards fossil fuels.

Meanwhile, volatility caused by the Iran war boosted earnings in the first half for Shell’s oil trading operations.

title: SK Hynix moves to calm market with US$29 bil share buy-back
article:
(Aug 19): SK Hynix Inc unveiled plans to buy back 40 trillion won (US$29 billion or $36.6 billion) of stock and return more of its profits to shareholders in an effort to calm worries about the durability of artificial intelligence (AI) spending.

The memory chipmaker said it will buy back as many as 24 million treasury shares between Aug 20 and Nov 19 and cancel them, according to a regulatory filing on Wednesday. It also boosted its shareholder return pledge to more than 50% of free cash flow, up from a previous target of within 50%. Its US shares rose as much as 7.1% in pre-market trading.

SK Hynix’s buy-back plan follows the US$26.5 billion it raised just a month ago in a US listing, which came around the height of market excitement around an AI rally. But since then, investors have cooled on the trade and begun demanding a handout.

“The size of this buy-back is a strong signal from SK Hynix and delivers something investors have been calling for, putting its growing cash pile to work and increasing shareholder returns,” said Josh Gilbert, an analyst at Etoro. “Lifting the returns target from within 50% of free cash flow to above 50% is the change that will still be relevant long after this week’s price action is forgotten.”

South Korea continues to be the focus of the Asian tech trade, after an investor frenzy that pushed market values of SK Hynix and home-grown rival Samsung Electronics Co to more than US$1 trillion each. The South Korean benchmark Kospi is still posting large daily swings, although the mountain of leveraged trades that drove record levels of volatility has started to unwind.

See also: LG Energy mulls supplying batteries for US drones in pivot

SK Hynix, a key supplier of high‑bandwidth memory chips to Nvidia Corp, joined a recent sell-off over worries that spending on AI hardware could be fleeting. SK Hynix shares declined on Wednesday in South Korea before the buy-back announcement, tracking losses in US semiconductor and other AI-related stocks as concerns over inflation and rising government debt kept bond yields elevated. The threat of higher borrowing costs is adding to market worries amid ongoing uncertainty over the Iran war.

“Buy-backs may offer a temporary ‘cushion’ for memory stocks, but the bigger driver remains interest rates,” said Gary Tan, a portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments. “Until long term yields stabilise, valuation and shareholder return support alone is unlikely to prevent continued volatility.”

title: Philippine peso hits record low as pressure on BSP to act grows
article:
(Aug19): The Philippine peso fell to a record low against the dollar as oil prices climbed, putting more pressure on the central bank to take action.

The peso fell as much as 0.3% to 61.995 per dollar, weakening past the previous all-time low of 61.850 set in July. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas said on Wednesday that it “intervenes to address disorderly market conditions and smooth extreme volatility, especially when these can accelerate inflation”.

Brent crude has jumped about 5% in four days, weighing on the peso as the Philippines imports almost all of its oil. Traders are now watching whether the currency will breach the level of 62 per dollar, placing further pressure on the central bank to respond.

The BSP “will probably be biased to hike rates again to defend the peso, but the impact of rates hikes to curb FX depreciation is diminishing”, said Wee Khoon Chong, senior Asia Pacific market strategist at BNY in Hong Kong. “With the dollar-peso breaching the previous top of 61.85 with minimal resistance, market and momentum is likely to drive it higher towards 62.00 and beyond.”

The peso has lost around 5% this year, making it one of Asia’s worst-performing currencies. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr said last week that the Philippines would not spend all its reserves to defend the peso, while foreign-exchange holdings have fallen almost 7% this year to US$103 billion.

See also: Yen remains on 160 watch despite Takaichi’s support for rate hike by BOJ

Ahead of its Aug 27 meeting, the BSP faces a tougher policy choice as the peso weakens and oil prices climb. The central bank has said it is prepared to step in if needed, with July inflation at 6.2%, well above its 3% target.

“The BSP may hike rates next week to stem inflation on the back of the movement in FX,” said Philip McNicholas, Asia sovereign strategist at Robeco in Singapore. “It may use FX intervention to smooth out aggressive moves, but should not go beyond that as it still wants the market to determine the level of peso.”

title: Copper holds loss as deliveries to LME mitigate supply crunch
article:
(Aug19): Copper declined while readily available stocks on the London Metal Exchange swelled to ease a historic squeeze on supplies.

On-warrant inventories jumped by more than 35,000 tonnes, the most since 2024, according to data released Wednesday. That followed inflows of more than 20,000 tonnes in the previous session, an increase to which Trafigura Group contributed a significant share, Bloomberg News reported.

The arrival of copper in LME warehouses relieves some pressure after stockpiles with the bourse were drained by a surge in shipments to the US. That crunch was driven largely by an arbitrage trade in anticipation of import tariffs but a deadline for the US Commerce Department’s recommendation to US President Donald Trump passed in June with no announcement.

The closely watched spread between copper for immediate delivery and delivery three months out dropped to US$207 a tonne Wednesday from a backwardation of as much as US$545 on Monday. Another key one-day price spread known as Tom/next also fell after spiking to levels last seen during a major squeeze in 2021.

Benchmark three-month copper futures on the LME fell 0.9% to trade at US$13,865.50 a tonne as of 10.04am in London. That followed a decline of 1.2% on Tuesday, which was the biggest one-day drop since July 23.

See also: Copper supply crunch sends key spread to highest since 2021

Elsewhere, China’s refined copper output rose 1.3% year on year to 1.285 million tonnes in July. A favourable import arbitrage is also encouraging more metal to flow into the country.
